name: The Man Who Sold the World

podcast.body: Released in 1970 and produced by Tony Visconti, this album saw Bowie refining his sound and rocking harder. Despite this, the album was initially a flop on both sides of the Atlantic, failing to chart in either the UK or US upon its original release. "The following year, on his 1970 LP The Man Who Sold the World, Bowie refined his sound with producer Tony Visconti and rocked harder, but the album was a flop on both sides of the Atlantic, failing to chart in either the UK or US."

podcast.body: Ten months after appearing in a gay magazine, Bowie appeared on this album's cover wearing a long, flowing blue dress, which he referred to as a "man's dress" designed by Mr. Fish. This was considered the most feminized image a rock star had presented to the world at that point, leading some stores to refuse to stock the album, resulting in copies with different covers. The album sold poorly in the US, with fewer than 1,500 copies moved between November 1970 and June 1971, primarily due to the controversial dress. Today, however, it is regarded as the pivotal moment where Bowie's artistic growth began to blossom and when he started to find his signature sound, marking the beginning of the Bowie known today. "This was the most feminized image a rock star the world had ever seen."

podcast.body: The original cover of this album, released in November 1970, featured Bowie reclining in a full-length blue dress he purchased from a boutique called Mr. Fish. This cover was poorly received in America, where many record stores refused to stock it, leading RCA Records to supply an alternative cover. Due to this controversy, the album sold only 1,395 copies in America between November 1970 and June 1971. "When Bowie released the album, The Man Who Sold the World, the original cover featured him reclining wearing this full-length blue dress."

podcast.body: This album featured Bowie on the cover wearing a flowing gown designed by British fashion maven Mr. Fish (Michael Fish). This look, displaying androgyny, was not encouraged in 1970, leading to certain stores in the US refusing to display the record and hurting sales until new editions with different covers were rushed out in places like the US and Germany. Inside the album, new songs indicated a significant creative opening for Bowie. "But Bowie didn't care, even as the controversy hurt sales."

podcast.body: This album was released in November 1970. Its original artwork was highly scandalous for 1970s Britain, featuring Bowie in a dress with hormone hair and what appeared to be a purse for his makeup. This image sparked outrage, as homosexuality had been a crime in the UK until 1967, leading hundreds of record stores to refuse to stock the album if that cover was used. As a result, the original artwork was suppressed for many years. "Still the album came up. November 1970, this is David Bowie, with the title track of The Man Who Sold the World."

podcast.body: This album's cover featured David Bowie wearing a flowing gown designed by Mr. Fish, also known as Michael Fish, a prominent British fashion maven. Bowie insisted on wearing the dress in public and to interviews, which was not widely encouraged in 1970. Certain US stores refused to display the record due to "a dude in a dress," causing controversy that hurt sales until new editions with different covers were quickly released in markets like the US and Germany. "Inside though, it was apparent that the floodgates had begun to open when it came to new songs."

podcast.body: David Bowie's 1971 album, considered his second rock and roll album, was recorded and mixed at Trident Studios in London. The liner notes highlighted Bowie as an emerging artist with a distinctiveness, describing the music as "unmistakably vintage Bowie" and the album as mirroring his "intense and vulnerable intelligence and ... sensuality." All songs on the album were written by Bowie, and it notably featured Ralph Mace on a Moog synthesizer. RCA promoted it as a "Dynaflex recording," a new manufacturing development aimed at improving sound quality and reducing record warpage. "This album, recorded at the onset of the decade, is a clear prognosis for the decade."
